text:
To the old elm, split by lightning
and half-rotten,
some green leaves have sprouted
with the April rains and the May sun.

The century-old elm on the hill
that the Duero licks! A yellowish moss
stains the whitish bark
of the worm-eaten, dusty trunk.

It will not be, like the singing poplars
that guard the road and the riverbank,
inhabited by brown nightingales.

An army of ants in file
climbs over it, and in its entrails
gray spiders weave their webs.

Before the woodcutter fells you, elm of the Duero,
with his axe, and the carpenter turns you
into a bell yoke,
a cart shaft, or a wagon yoke;
before tomorrow, red in the hearth,
you burn in some wretched hut
by the roadside;
before a whirlwind uproots you
and the breath of the white sierras snaps you;
before the river pushes you to the sea
through valleys and ravines,
elm, I want to note in my notebook
the grace of your newly green branch.

My heart waits
also, toward the light and toward life,
for another miracle of spring.

translation.title: To a Dry Elm
translation.editorial_note: The translation preserves the elm's successive possible fates, the Duero and white sierras, and the speaker's final hope that the green branch foreshadows a miracle in his own heart.
